summary: The signal calls `Number()` and `parseInt` "explicit casts", but the concept's own misconception says a cast does not convert a value, and these two do convert.
rationale: `Number(x)` and `parseInt(s)` are runtime conversions. `as` is a compile-time assertion that changes nothing at runtime. Putting them in one bucket next to the misconception "Assuming a cast converts a value rather than silencing the type checker" invites the lesson generator to teach that `Number()` doesn't convert, or to grade a correct answer as wrong. The signals `type or interface declarations` and `null or undefined checks and optional chaining` also appear in almost every TypeScript file, so they will over-map; the signals should point at decision points instead.

It is only wrong for block-bodied functions in JS/TS, Python, Java and similar languages, so it has to say which case it means. summary: The concept teaches "closures capture variables, not values" but never explains why stale closures look like snapshots, so a lesson using both will seem to contradict itself.
rationale: Stale closures in React-style code happen because each render creates new const bindings. An effect captured the binding from an earlier render, which never changes, so it behaves like a snapshot. Without that explanation, a lesson built from objective 2 (capture variables) and objective 3 (stale closures) can confuse learners or graders. The signal "React hooks capturing props or state" is also framework lock-in and could be rephrased neutrally, e.g. "UI hooks or effects with dependency arrays".

summary: No concept anywhere in the graph covers dates, times and time zones, a frequent and costly class of bugs in the apps this product targets.

Right now the mapper would squeeze them into values-and-types or web.serialization, which can't teach the topic properly. It fits a 5–10 minute lesson and is much more common in real PRs than several existing nodes.

summary: "Assuming iteration order is irrelevant or random in all languages" is muddled. It does not state one clear wrong belief, and it misses the common real bug.
rationale: "Irrelevant" is not a belief about ordering. The dangerous mistake usually goes the other way: developers rely on insertion order because JavaScript Map and Python dict keep it, then get burned by Go maps (randomized), Java HashMap (unspecified), Postgres jsonb (keys reordered), or plain JS objects (integer-like keys sorted first). The __proto__ item describes a behavior, not a belief. The key-equality item should say it is about reference identity.

Assuming iteration order is irrelevant or random in all languages

after: Expecting object or array keys in a Map or Set to be matched by their contents rather than by reference

summary: The summary says maps and sets are always hash-based and constant-time. That is imprecise, and wrong for common non-JS structures.
rationale: Hash tables give expected (average) O(1) lookups, with worst-case linear time under collisions (the basis of hash-flooding DoS). Sorted maps such as Java TreeMap, C++ std::map and Rust BTreeMap are tree-based with O(log n) lookup. Learners on other stacks, and the lesson generator, should not treat constant time as a guarantee.
before: Hash-based structures that answer 'have I seen this key?' and 'what value belongs to this key?' in roughly constant time.
after: Key-based structures, usually hash tables, that answer 'have I seen this key?' and 'what value belongs to this key?' in expected constant time; sorted tree-based maps trade that for ordered keys and logarithmic lookup.

This regularly breaks 'one active row per user' style invariants that developers think the constraint enforces.

rationale: 'Never changes row counts' is vague: compared to what? The precise wrong belief is that a LEFT JOIN returns exactly one row per left-table row. Putting a filter on the right table in WHERE instead of ON drops the unmatched rows. That is one of the most common join bugs and fits the predict and trace modes well. 'Adding DISTINCT instead of fixing the join' should state the belief behind it.

summary: The composite-index item is ambiguous, the lock item is not stated as a belief, and the common Postgres assumption that foreign keys are indexed automatically is missing.
rationale: 'Works for any column order' can mean the order of predicates in the WHERE clause, and that order really doesn't matter. A grader or lesson generator could therefore teach the opposite of what is intended. The real belief is that an index on (a, b) serves queries that filter only on b. Postgres 18 skip scan helps in narrow low-cardinality cases, so the wording should say 'generally'. 'Forgetting…' describes a lapse, not a belief, and should say how Postgres actually behaves: a plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes, while CONCURRENTLY does not but cannot run inside a transaction block. Many migration runners wrap every migration in a transaction. Postgres, unlike MySQL InnoDB, does not index the referencing column of a foreign key. That causes slow joins and slow cascading deletes, and it is one of the most common real index bugs.

summary: One item is an action rather than a belief, and the most common ORM transaction bug is missing: a query that uses the global client instead of the transaction handle.
rationale: 'Holding a transaction open across slow network calls' names a mistake but not the belief behind it or its cost. The cost is held locks and a pinned pool connection. With callback-style ORM transactions, AI-generated code often calls the outer client (for example `db.x` instead of `tx.x`) inside the callback, and those writes quietly run outside the transaction. It is easy to spot in a diff and is worth teaching. 'Sequential awaits' is also tied to JS wording when a language-neutral version works just as well.

summary: The counter item is an action rather than a belief, the default-isolation item gives no concrete defaults, and the FOR UPDATE phantom-insert belief is missing.
rationale: 'Incrementing counters by reading into application memory first' describes code, not a belief. The belief is that read-modify-write in the app is safe when an atomic UPDATE is available. Stating the real defaults (Postgres READ COMMITTED, MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ) makes the item precise and gradeable. Many developers think SELECT ... FOR UPDATE prevents concurrent inserts. It does not lock rows that don't exist yet, which is exactly how write skew and duplicate-booking bugs get through. Another common belief is that SERIALIZABLE needs no retry logic, and the existing retry signal has no misconception to pair with it.

SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0` with an affected-row check, not locks or serializable isolation. Leaving it out teaches heavier tools first. Under READ COMMITTED each statement takes a new snapshot, so two SELECTs in one transaction can see different data. summary: The misconceptions miss the main Postgres migration outage (a lock that queues and blocks all traffic), and the NOT NULL item points at a harmless failure rather than the real risk.
rationale: In Postgres, adding a NOT NULL column with no default to a populated table fails with an error, so nothing is silently damaged. Since Postgres 11, adding a column with a constant default is metadata-only. The changes that cause outages are different. An ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so it waits behind any long transaction and blocks every later read and write on that table. SET NOT NULL and a validated foreign-key add both scan the table while holding a strong lock. Two items are also phrased as actions, not beliefs, and the brief's intended objective about long-locking steps has nothing to anchor it. People also wrongly believe that rolling back or running a down migration brings back dropped data.

Adding a NOT NULL column without a default to a populated table
Editing a migration that has already run elsewhere
after: Believing the migration and the new application code go live at the same instant, so old code never runs against the new schema

Believing SET NOT NULL or adding a foreign key to a large existing table is a cheap metadata change, when it scans the table while holding a strong lock (NOT VALID then VALIDATE avoids the long lock)

Believing a down migration or deploy rollback restores data removed by dropping a column or table

check.note: Checked against Postgres behavior: a NOT NULL column without a default fails loudly on a populated table, and lock queueing behind long transactions is the real outage. One simplification: for SET NOT NULL, the fast path is first adding and validating a CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) constraint (PG12+); NOT VALID applies to CHECK and foreign-key constraints.

summary: Injection bundles SQL, shell, HTML and LLM prompt injection into one concept even though prompt injection has no equivalent of parameterization, and it duplicates XSS with security.web-vulnerabilities.
rationale: For SQL, shell and HTML the unifying lesson is to use an API that keeps data separate from code (bound parameters, argument arrays, context-aware encoding). Prompt injection has no such separation: current guidance (OWASP LLM01) says it cannot be reliably prevented, only contained. Teaching it alongside 'structural separation as a defense' suggests that delimiters work. Four sink families is also too much for one 5–10 minute lesson. XSS is claimed both here (dangerouslySetInnerHTML signal) and in web-vulnerabilities (user-provided HTML signal), so a mapper cannot tell the two apart. OWASP files XSS under Injection, so keep XSS here, move prompt injection to its own concept (see new-concept finding), and remove XSS from web-vulnerabilities.

summary: Two of three entries describe practices, not wrong beliefs, and the list misses the precise false beliefs behind leaked secrets and containers that won't stop.
rationale: 'Baking secrets into image layers' and 'Running as root without need' say what people do but not the belief a lesson should correct. Stated as beliefs: a secret removed in a later layer, or passed via ARG/ENV, is gone from the image (it persists in earlier layers, image history or config); and root inside a container is harmless because the container is isolated (without user namespaces, it is host UID 0). A common real failure is also missing: PID 1 gets no default signal handling, so a shell-form CMD or an app without a SIGTERM handler doesn't shut down cleanly.

summary: Nothing in the graph covers how short-lived, replaceable instances (serverless functions, autoscaled servers, containers) run code, even though that model causes many production bugs in the target Next.js/Postgres stack.
rationale: The brief's 'processes/threads' is framed here around long-running Node servers, but most target learners deploy to serverless or edge runtimes. Common, costly bugs there have no concept to map to: un-awaited work cut off after the response is returned, module-scope state assumed to be global, per-instance DB pools exhausting Postgres connections, and edge vs Node runtime limits. Grep finds no serverless or runtime-lifecycle coverage anywhere in the data. This concept also takes the lifecycle half of processes-and-threads and gives containers the right prerequisite.

summary: For novices, the 2-root graph plus the 0.35 unmet threshold means every other concept gets the full penalty, so the two roots are strongly favoured and prerequisite edges barely change ranking.

So 51/51 non-root concepts take the full −0.15, while systems.networking-basics and fundamentals.values-and-types take none and also get readiness 1.0 instead of 0.44–0.61. As a result, networking-basics mapped at significance 0.40, or values-and-types at 0.46, outranks a central web.authn-vs-authz gap at significance 0.9 (0.656). Also stop adding roots that have broad signals (see the networking-basics finding).
